beats.text: Your friend's success stings. That doesn't make you a bad friend!
In a classic experiment, men brought a friend to a word-guessing game. They could give easy clues or hard ones.
Then the researchers said the game measured intelligence. Here's the twist.
They gave their friend harder clues than a stranger! In ten of thirteen sessions.
When it's not your thing, you cheer for your friend. When it is your thing, their win can feel like your loss.
What helps: celebrate anyway. In studies on good news, an excited, curious reply went with closer relationships.
So feel the sting. Then say: tell me everything!

ask: TAG A FRIEND YOU'RE PROUD OF.
sources: Tesser & Smith (1980), Some effects of task relevance and friendship on helping: You don't always help the one you like, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 16(6), 582–590 – men brought a friend; Password-style game, clues could be easy or hard; when the task was described as measuring important verbal skills, the stranger was helped more than the friend in 10 of 13 sessions; when described as unimportant, the friend was helped more in 10 of 13 sessions.
Tesser (1988), Toward a self-evaluation maintenance model of social behavior, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 21.

Gable, Reis, Impett & Asher (2004), What do you do when things go right? The intrapersonal and interpersonal benefits of sharing positive events, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 87(2), 228–245 – active-constructive (enthusiastic, engaged) responses to good news went with higher intimacy, satisfaction and trust; correlational.
